title: When the Past Knocks
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 11 of 40
content:
The past knocked at the tea shop door just before sunrise.

Iroh was in the kitchen when the sound came. Three measured knocks. Not a customer. Not a delivery.

I was carrying a tray down the stairs when he looked toward the front of the shop.

“Stay upstairs,” he said.

“That is not a good sign.”

“It is a cautious sign.”

“You are cautious when it is a good sign too.”

He placed the tray on the counter. “Please.”

The word made me stop.

Iroh opened the door.

A man in a faded Fire Nation uniform stood in the street. He was older than Iroh by a few years, his face weathered and his left hand missing two fingers. He stared at the tea shop sign.

“I did not know you were here,” he said.

“Many people do not,” Iroh replied.

“I heard.”

The man looked past him and saw me on the stairs.

“You have help.”

“I do.”

“A life.”

Iroh's expression tightened. “I am trying.”

The man laughed without humor. “You always were good at trying after the damage was done.”

I descended the last steps. Iroh glanced at me, not ordering me back this time.

“Would you like tea?” he asked the visitor.

“No.”

“Then why have you come?”

The man reached into his coat and pulled out a folded letter. “Your nephew is looking for you.”

Iroh took the letter but did not open it.

“He knows where I am,” he said.

“He wants you at the palace.”

“He knows where to send a messenger.”

“He sent me.”

The room grew smaller.

The man looked at Iroh with a mixture of anger and exhaustion. “The new Fire Lord needs someone who understands the old army. There are generals refusing to disband. Governors who still answer to the wrong people. He thinks you can help.”

“Can I?”

“You know them.”

“Knowing is not the same as controlling.”

“It is more than he has.”

Iroh turned the letter over in his hand.

I watched him. The tea shop, the room upstairs, the corner table—everything that had begun to feel stable appeared suddenly fragile.

“How long would you be gone?” I asked.

The visitor looked at me. Iroh did too.

“I do not know,” Iroh said.

The answer hurt more than I expected.

“Then you should go,” I said.

Iroh's eyes sharpened. “You do not have to decide for me.”

“I’m not.” I looked at the letter. “I’m saying the people who need you may not have another choice.”

“And what about you?”

“I am not the person who needs you to save them.”

His face went still.

The visitor shifted near the door. “I will wait outside.”

He stepped into the street and closed the door.

Iroh remained behind the counter.

“That was not what I wanted to hear,” he said.

“I know.”

“You believe I should leave.”

“I believe you should choose. I don’t want you to stay because you think I’ll fall apart without you.”

“You would not.”

“I might be lonely.”

“That is different.”

“I know.”

He set the letter down. “I am tired of being useful only when the world is burning.”

The confession was quiet and devastating.

“Then tell them no,” I said.

“Can I?”

“You can decide that.”

“If I say no, people may suffer.”

“If you say yes, you may disappear into a life that has already taken everything from you.”

Iroh looked at the tea shelves. “You make it sound like there is a right answer.”

“There might not be.”

He closed his eyes.

I moved around the counter. “I don’t want to lose you. But I don’t want to become the reason you betray what you believe is right.”

“You are not a reason to betray anything.”

“Then don’t treat me like one.”

He opened his eyes. “You are asking me to be honest.”

“Yes.”

“Even if honesty changes things?”

“Especially then.”

Iroh took my hand. His palm felt warm, but his fingers trembled.

“I love you,” he said.

The words were not a distraction. They were not a promise that everything would be easy.

“I love you too,” I replied.

“I may need to leave for a time.”

“I know.”

“I may decide I cannot.”

“I know.”

“I do not know what I will choose.”

“Then choose honestly.”

His eyes filled.

He lifted my hand and kissed it. Then he pulled me around the counter and held me against his chest.

“Stay with me while I decide?” he asked.

“Yes.”

The visitor waited outside. The kettle began to whistle. The city woke around the tea shop.

Iroh did not open the letter immediately.

For one more cup, he let the past wait.

The visitor returned after sunrise. This time, he had changed out of the uniform. He wore a plain brown coat and carried no weapon that I could see.

Iroh opened the door. “You have come back.”

“I have.”

“Would you like tea?”

The man hesitated. “I said no yesterday.”

“You may change your mind.”

“That is not how the army worked.”

“The tea shop is not the army.”

The man entered.

I served him jasmine. He held the cup but did not drink.

“My name is Ren,” he said.

I gave him my name.

He nodded. “I wanted to know who was here.”

Iroh sat across from him. “You have seen us.”

“I wanted to know whether you would stay when I said my brother died.”

Iroh's hands rested around his cup. “I did not know whether I would.”

“You stayed.”

“Yes.”

Ren finally drank the tea. His face changed, not with pleasure exactly, but with recognition.

“My brother liked this,” he said.

“Many people do.”

“He said it made the city feel less gray.”

Iroh looked toward the jasmine vines outside. “He was not wrong.”

Ren sat for a long time. He did not ask forgiveness. Iroh did not offer it. They shared tea and the difficult shape of being alive after someone else was not.

When Ren left, he placed a folded paper on the table. It was a list of names: soldiers missing, homes damaged, families still waiting for news.

“He wants you to read it,” Iroh said.

“Will you?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it makes you feel guilty?”

“Especially then. Guilt is not the same as responsibility, but it can point toward it.”

I looked at the list. “What will you do?”

“I will bring it to the people who can help. I will not promise what I cannot provide.”

“And then you will leave.”

“Yes.”

The word held the future.

That evening, I helped Iroh pack. He needed clothes, letters, maps, tea, and the small game board he carried everywhere. I folded his shirts while he argued with the amount of socks required for three weeks.

“You need more than two pairs,” I said.

“I am traveling with a tea chest.”

“The tea chest cannot replace socks.”

“You underestimate its versatility.”

I added three pairs to the bag.

Iroh watched me from the desk. “You are very comfortable giving orders.”

“Only about socks.”

“A narrow authority.”

“A necessary one.”

When the bag was ready, he sat on the edge of the bed. I stood between his knees.

“I do not want to leave you,” he said.

“I know.”

“I do not want to leave this room.”

“I know.”

“I do not want to become the man I was because people ask for him.”

I touched his face. “Then do not go alone.”

“You should not have to follow me.”

“I am not following.”

His eyes searched mine.

“I am choosing to come with you,” I said. “If there is room.”

Iroh's breath caught. “There is always room for you.”

“Do not say always lightly.”

“I do not.”

Iroh asked whether I wanted him to stay close. I said yes and leaned my head against his shoulder. We talked quietly about his journey and the days ahead, letting the rest of the night remain private.

We stayed together in the quiet while my last night in Ba Sing Se settled around us.

At dawn, the letter lay open on the counter.

Iroh had written back: I WILL COME. I WILL LISTEN. I WILL NOT PROMISE TO BE WHAT I WAS.

I read it over his shoulder.

“That is a good letter,” I said.

“It is a beginning.”

I took his hand.

Together, I carried the tea chests into the street.

The city was still gray with dawn. Iroh locked the shop behind me, then looked up at the room above it.

“You may stay,” he said.

“I know.”

“You may leave.”

“I know.”

“You may choose either without it changing what you mean to me.”

I took his hand. “Then I choose the road.”

He squeezed my fingers.

The road opened beyond the gate, pale beneath the morning rain.

I walked beside Iroh.

The road waited for neither permission nor certainty.

I followed it.

Iroh followed beside me.

The tea chests bumped against the cart. The road smelled of wet stone and green leaves.
